extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political economy / classical economics; historians of price and monetary theory
extracted.subtask_description: Expository principles and interpretive guidelines for analyzing the real value of precious metals (especially silver) relative to corn and labour, and for interpreting historical price data. Focuses on causes of price changes, measurement of real value, and pitfalls in using historical statutes and price series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination of silver's value by supply and demand in the commercial world
rubrics_metrics.description: The great market for silver is the commercial and civilized part of the world. The value of silver depends on the relation between its supply and the demand of that market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three exhaustive combinations: (1) if demand increases while supply does not, the value of silver rises and a given quantity exchanges for more corn (money price of corn becomes cheaper); (2) if supply increases more than demand, silver becomes cheaper and the money price of corn becomes dearer; (3) if supply increases nearly in the same proportion as demand, the exchange between silver and corn remains nearly the same. Use these cases to reason about long-term trends in silver relative to corn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corn (grain) as the preferred measure of the real value of silver
rubrics_metrics.description: Corn, or the common vegetable food of the people, is a more accurate measure of value than other commodities because its production is principally the product of human industry and it constitutes the principal subsistence of the labourer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare silver to corn when judging real value: equal quantities of corn more nearly represent equal quantities of labour across different stages of improvement than other unmanufactured commodities. The money price of labour depends much more on the average money price of corn than on butcher’s meat or other rude produce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labour is the ultimate or real measure of value
rubrics_metrics.description: Labour, and not any particular commodity, is the real measure of the value both of silver and of all other commodities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing real value, translate commodity prices into the quantity of labour they represent. Beware of using single commodities other than corn as measures, since their labour-content can vary more widely across societies and stages of improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish causes of increases in the quantity of precious metals
rubrics_metrics.description: The quantity of the precious metals may increase either from (a) the increased abundance of mines which supply them, or (b) from the increased wealth of the people (greater annual produce of labour).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These causes have different effects: (a) discovery of more abundant mines necessarily diminishes the value of the metals (more metal for same quantity of goods), while (b) increased national wealth raises demand for coin and plate and does not necessarily diminish the metals' value. Analyze which cause is operative before inferring value changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of political/security improvements and exhaustion of mines on silver value
rubrics_metrics.description: Greater security and improvement increase industry and demand for precious metals; exhaustion of known mines makes supply scarcer and raises the expense of working them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret historical rises in silver's value in light of increased demand from improving societies and/or decreased supply from exhausted mines. Both factors may act together; examine evidence of mining productivity and social/political stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious with nominal sums and coinage alterations when reading statutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Alterations in the coin (the quantity of silver contained in a nominal sum) and the legislature's repeated use of the same nominal sums across centuries can mislead interpretations of real prices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a statute fixes prices in shillings/pence across long periods, check how much actual silver that nominal sum contained at each date. Do not assume identical nominal sums imply equal real value without adjusting for coin debasement or recoinage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mistaking conversion price (payment-in-kind exchange price) for actual market price
rubrics_metrics.description: In places where rents were paid in kind, landlords sometimes reserved the option to take a money payment; the money sum used in conversion (conversion price) was often set below market price for tenant safety and thus is not the true market price.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not take recorded conversion prices (e.g., Scottish examples) as market prices. Seek evidence of actual market transactions or institutional valuations (public fiars) rather than conversion figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Being misled by slovenly transcriptions of assize statutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Some ancient statutes of assize were imperfectly transcribed, with copiers often recording only the lowest few price steps and omitting the remainder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify statute texts against reliable manuscripts; beware conclusions drawn from truncated transcriptions (e.g., assuming the middle price was X because later price ranges were omitted). Consider the statute's stated pattern (‘et sic deinceps’) indicating continuity beyond copied examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inferring ordinary prices from occasional extremes is fallacious
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers have sometimes taken very low or very high recorded prices in particular years as representative of ordinary prices, despite these being exceptional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat isolated extreme prices (very high during famine, very low during exceptional plenty) as atypical. Use averaged series and context (political disorder, disrupted trade) to infer ordinary or average prices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geography, transport costs, and domestic supply strongly affect corn prices but not silver equally
rubrics_metrics.description: In great towns and rich commercial countries (e.g., Holland, Genoa), corn is dear because it must be brought from distant countries; silver’s real cost is nearly the same across places but corn’s varies with transport and supply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain regional/city differences in money prices of corn by transport and availability rather than by assuming differing real value of silver. When comparing regions, adjust for carriage, insurance, and local scarcity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Price of labour relates principally to subsistence and the country's state of advancement
rubrics_metrics.description: The money price of labour depends much more on the average money price of corn (the labourer’s subsistence) and on whether a country is advancing, stationary, or declining than on its absolute wealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare labour prices across countries taking into account subsistence costs and the dynamic condition (growth vs stagnation). Use migration frequency and demand for labour as empirical indicators (e.g., emigration frequency difference between Scotland and England).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative values of commodities differ in poor vs rich societies (necessaries vs unmanufactured produce)
rubrics_metrics.description: In poor or uncultivated countries, unmanufactured commodities (cattle, poultry, game) may be cheap relative to corn because they require little labour to acquire; this cheapness reflects low real value of those commodities, not high real value of silver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid interpreting low nominal prices of non-subsistence goods as evidence of high silver value. Instead assess real labour embodied in those goods and the local abundance relative to demand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavior of necessaries and luxuries across economic cycles
rubrics_metrics.description: When we are in want of necessaries, their real price (quantity of labour they command) rises in times of poverty and distress and sinks in times of opulence and prosperity; luxuries behave oppositely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect the real price of necessaries to increase under scarcity and decrease under abundance; do not assume all prices move the same way during economic changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat on historical price series and their representativeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Collections of ancient prices (e.g., Fleetwood, Dupré de St Maur) often record years notable for extraordinary dearness or cheapness, and thus may not provide a complete or unbiased picture of ordinary prices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using historical price compilations, examine sample selection (are they biased toward extremes?), temporal coverage (gaps), and whether averages across suitable intervals are presented. Prefer averaged twelve-year divisions or institutional valuations where available.
